theory_content: In a zero-based budget, income minus every allocation equals zero — including the allocations to saving and investing. Nothing is "left over", because leftovers are what get spent. It takes about twenty minutes a month and reliably surfaces the 10-20% of spending that nobody would defend if asked about it directly.

theory_title: Which costs you can actually change
theory_content: Fixed costs — rent, EMIs, insurance, school fees — are set for months or years and are the hardest to cut in a crisis. Variable costs — food delivery, travel, shopping — move immediately. Most people try to fix a budget by attacking variable costs, when the real problem is usually one fixed commitment signed a year ago.

theory_title: A starting shape, not a law
theory_content: Fifty percent of take-home to needs, thirty to wants, twenty to savings and debt repayment. It is useful as a first check rather than a target: in expensive Indian cities rent alone can be 40%, which means the split has to be redrawn rather than abandoned. If needs exceed 60%, the problem is housing or transport, not coffee.

Insurance premiums, festival spending, school fees and the annual holiday are not emergencies — they are predictable costs that arrive in lumps. A sinking fund sets aside one-twelfth each month so the lump is already funded when it lands. Most "unexpected" expenses are only unexpected in timing, not in existence.
